lines: Run the exact same command on two versions of the same engine, one update apart.
On the older version, the plan shows nothing about memory and disk traffic at all.
On the newer version, that same line shows up on its own, completely unasked for.
Nothing about the query changed between those two runs, and nothing extra was requested either time.
So why would the exact same command print more information, just because it ran on a newer version?
answer: The engine's own default for what gets shown changed, between those two versions.
That's a real, dated decision the project made about what to show automatically, not a bug, and not the planner reasoning about this one query in particular.

lines: The newer version's own documentation states the change plainly: asking it to actually run the query now also turns on detailed memory and disk reporting, by default.
The older version never did that. Asking it to run the query only ever showed timing, nothing about memory or disk, unless that reporting was requested separately.
That's exactly what this topic's own older instance still requires, side by side with the newer one on the same machine.
Every engine's plan carries two numbers for the same spot: what the planner guessed beforehand, and what actually came out once the query ran.
Here, the planner guessed a little over one thousand rows for one spot in the plan.
Two thousand rows actually came out of that same spot — a real, naturally occurring gap, not a constructed worst case.
This same chapter already measured a closely related question: whether an operator ran within its own memory budget, or had to spill extra data to disk.
That measurement read straight off a few specific numbers the engine itself printed, once asked.
Every engine answers that same question somewhere in its own output. Only the name of the field, and where it shows up, actually changes.
Five different engines format all of this five different ways, with five different names for closely related things.
Facing an unfamiliar plan from any one of them, where should your eye actually land first?
answer: Wherever the real number diverges furthest from what was expected.
A huge but expected count isn't a problem on its own, and a small spot run over and over can matter more than a big one run just once.

lines: Ask one particular engine for its cost-aware plan, and its own estimate is sitting right there in the text.
A range of one million rows, printed directly on the exact spot in the plan that produces them.
No separate screen needed to see that number. It's part of the plan itself.
What that plan text can't tell you is what the run actually did once it finished.
For that, look somewhere else entirely: a comfortable run reports nothing spilled to memory or disk, read straight from that engine's own separate dashboard and its programming interface.
A memory-constrained run of a similar job reports a real, measured amount spilled to both memory and disk — not a hypothetical number, an observed one.
A completed stage's own reported numbers include how many bytes it moved between machines, and separately, how many bytes it had to spill to memory or disk.
Which one of those actually tells you a stage ran out of its own memory?
answer: Moving data between stages is ordinary, expected work in every healthy run. Spilling is a separate, specific signal that only shows up once an operator actually runs out of the memory it was given.

lines: One engine's own documentation describes a plan that shows the processing time spent in each stage, right alongside the relative cost of each individual step inside it.
Both of those numbers sit inline in the same plan text.
No separate screen is needed to see where the time actually went.
A different engine names this information with its own dedicated screens.
One screen reports how many pieces of a table actually got scanned, against how many pieces existed in total.
A separate screen reports how much data had to spill, broken out by whether it spilled locally or somewhere further away.
A fourth engine draws its own plan as a picture instead of text: boxes for each stage, with lines connecting them.
The estimated number of rows moving between stages sits on those connecting lines, not inside the boxes themselves.
That same engine also names, in its own words, spilling to disk as a specific cause of a query slowing down dramatically.
Five engines, five vocabularies, and still one fixed order worth checking regardless of which one is in front of you.

Start with the biggest gap between what was expected and what actually happened. Then a spot run far more times than expected. Then any sign of spilling. Then whichever single spot is simply the slowest or the widest.
Learn that one order once, and every new engine you meet is just a new set of field names hung on the same four questions.
One spot in a plan reports an expected count of five hundred.
The run actually produces fifty thousand. Is that estimate close, or badly off?
answer: Badly off, and worth investigating first.
A hundred-times gap between what was expected and what actually happened is exactly the kind of divergence this topic's own checking order puts at the very top, on any engine.

lines: A stage reports a large number of bytes moved between machines, and a separate spilled-bytes number sitting at exactly zero.
Did that stage run out of memory?
answer: No. A zero spilled-bytes number means it stayed within its own budget.
Moving data between stages is ordinary, expected work on its own. Spilling is a separate, specific signal, and this stage's own number says it simply never happened here.
